job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Tara Jensen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live in a student hall in Aarhus and my day usually starts with a run, then a bike to campus. I'm doing a master's in cybersecurity after my bachelor's in software engineering, so I'm in lectures or labs, and I'm trying to get through a project on securing delivery tracking systems. Last summer I did three months at a logistics software company, mostly testing. I chose cybersecurity because when I looked at job ads, it was the one that kept turning up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's about what I expected. At work I'd say the tools are helpful for routine stuff, like explaining an error, but you still have to check them. To friends I'd say good, because it means my degree stays worth something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the comfortable version. Cybersecurity needs people who understand what's going on, and AI creates more attacks too. I still have about fifteen thousand in loans and no offer, but the market for my field is decent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the master's in June and apply to about fifteen companies, mainly security firms and banks. I'd keep using AI to explain things I'm stuck on, not to write my work. And I'd do a security certificate, because employers ask for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm. I'm not worried about the job disappearing. I'm a bit tense about the first job, because everybody wants one with a name on it, and I haven't got one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the market look like to you for first jobs in security?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boyfriend Anders, who's a carpenter apprentice, says I worry too much and that there's always work. He's right in his world. In mine, there are a lot of people applying to the same few places.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you describe your approach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My plan is to be useful rather than clever. Practical, a bit boring, someone who writes the test that catches the bug. I'd be fine being that.

I'd tell friends my degree **keeps its worth**.
think: Cybersecurity needs **people who understand**, and AI creates more attacks too.
I still owe about **fifteen thousand** and have no offer.
do: Finish the master's in June and apply to about **fifteen** security firms and banks.
Use AI to **explain** errors, not to write my work.
Do a **security certificate** employers ask for.
feel: I feel **fairly calm**, with some tension about the first job.

Her boyfriend **Anders** is relaxed, but she knows her market is crowded.

steps.text: Finish the cybersecurity master's in June
Apply to about fifteen security firms and banks
Complete a recognised security certificate before applying

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to change a lot of jobs, and some of my friends should start paying attention. At work I'd say AI will take over routine testing and monitoring, and the interesting work will be reviewing it. I'd be careful not to sound too sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my internship was mostly testing, and that's high on the list of tasks software takes. I think entry-level work shrinks and the bar for starting rises. But security keeps its human side, because someone has to decide what's a real threat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get certified, join a student capture-the-flag team and apply to places that need analysts, not just testers. I'd start using AI tools more often, for log checking and writing reports, because everyone else will. And I'd keep my costs down with a cheap flat share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, I'd say. It's not a disaster for me, but it's another thing to think about when I already have loans and no offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pick where to apply?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask each firm how it uses AI and how many juniors it hires. If they hire fewer, I'd go where they still hire, like banks and the public sector. I'm not first to jump, but I try to jump when it's proven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your course is most exposed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My course mate Sofie, who's doing pure software development. She's got more exposure than I do and she's frightened. I'd tell her to look at security or testing of AI systems, which is a new category.

say: I'd say AI will take over **routine testing** and the work will be reviewing it.
I'd try not to sound **too sure**.
think: My internship was mostly **testing**, which software takes early.
The **bar for starting** rises, but humans still decide what's a real threat.

Apply for **analyst** roles, not just testing.
Use AI more for **log checking** and reports.
feel: I feel **uneasy**: it's one more thing on top of loans.
S1.quote: I'm not first to jump, but I try to jump when it's proven.

She worries about her classmate **Sofie** more than herself.

steps.text: Join the university capture-the-flag team and finish a security certificate
Apply for security analyst roles at banks and public bodies
Use AI for log checks and report drafts at work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say two years is too short to cope, and the biggest worry is what happens to people like me who haven't started. I'd say governments and firms should be open about what's coming. I'd also keep working, because quitting doesn't help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be scared. Cybersecurity is thinking work, and a clever system could do it better than me. The one thing that might hold is defending against AI itself, but I don't know if that's a job for people or for more AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for everything, including hands-on infrastructure roles, like securing factories and power. I'd live as cheaply as I can, move back to my parents' house, and ask my dad, who manages a bank branch, about any openings. And I'd stay up to date on the tools so I'm no worse than anyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. It doesn't feel real, and then it does. Anders would tell me to come and work with him, because carpentry is hands-on, and I'd laugh and also think about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it mean to change plans after four years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've been planning this career for four years and I'm not a person who changes plans easily. If I did change it, I'd want a reason, like a salary that actually covers the loans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really consider carpentry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a hybrid. I'd learn a skilled trade at weekends and keep applying for security jobs during the week. The three-year gap for robots is a small mercy, which gives me some years to prepare for hands-on work.

I'd keep working, because **quitting** doesn't help.
think: Cybersecurity is **thinking work**, and a clever system could do it better.
Defending against AI itself might hold, but I'm **not sure** it's for people.
do: Apply for everything, including **infrastructure** roles in factories and power.

Learn a **skilled trade** at weekends while applying.
feel: I feel **alarmed**; it doesn't feel real, and then it does.
S2.quote: I've been planning this career for four years and I'm not a person who changes plans easily.
fieldNote: Tara is **steady** in ordinary times and shaken here.
She sees the **three-year gap** for robots as a small mercy and plans a trade.
Anders's **carpentry** offer is half a joke and half an option.

steps.text: Apply for infrastructure security roles in factories and power utilities
Move back to my parents' house to cut costs
Learn a skilled trade at weekends alongside job applications
Save every spare coin to cover the loans

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to prepare if people actually do. At work I'd say learn the tools and the limits. To friends I'd say, don't count on the job you pictured at eighteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be twenty-nine, with maybe four years' experience in security. After that it's a gamble. I'd have savings and choices, though, which is more than I'd have in the two-year version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, take the first security job, save about a quarter of my pay and keep learning the AI tools at work. I'd study something that adds a second option, like industrial control systems, which are hands-on and slower to change. Maybe get a trade qualification at evening classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. I like having a number of years rather than a sudden date. It's the difference between a storm warning and a storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner than planned?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to two people each year who are a bit ahead of me, like my lecturer and my old manager at the logistics firm. If either says their team is cut, I'd move earlier. It's not very bold, but it's how I do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would family money come into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably my parents' help. Dad would pay a deposit, but I'd rather not touch it. If I can stay independent for five years, I'd feel I'd earned my own way.

say: I'd say five years is **enough to prepare** if people actually do.
I'd tell friends not to count on the job they pictured at **eighteen**.
think: I'd be twenty-nine with about **four years** of experience before a gamble.
I'd have **savings and choices**, which is more than in the two-year version.

Study **industrial control systems**, which are hands-on and slower to change.
Take evening classes for a **trade qualification**.

steps.text: Take the first security analyst job and save a quarter of each pay

Learn the employer's AI tools as colleagues start using them
Talk to my lecturer and former manager each year about changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and not to waste it. I'd tell friends to build skills they could use in more than one job. At work I'd say we'd better keep an eye on what the tools can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd be thirty-four and settled, maybe leading a small security team that supervises AI systems. The job will be different, but I'd have eight or nine years in it. I'd say I'm fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish the master's, take a security job, save, and buy a flat with Anders when we're about thirty. I'd learn the AI tools as they become standard, probably within a few years of my colleagues. And I'd get a trade certificate on the side, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a small cloud. I'd worry about my parents' retirement and the pension systems, but about my work, no.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your plans with Anders look over ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably ask Anders whether he wants to start his own carpentry firm and whether my security skills could help. Together we could have a small business that's hands-on and also uses the tools. It's a nice thought, and ten years is long enough to try it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does that long window make you less careful?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I think a decade of change would be a lot, but I'd handle it. I'd just have to keep reminding myself that planning isn't the same as worrying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I could handle five or ten years because I'd plan, but two years would hit me before I'd had a real job. What would help is clear information from firms about hiring, loan terms that bend, and a chance to try a trade.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume graduates in tech are rich. I owe fifteen thousand, I'm not sure of a job and I still pay my share of the rent. I'm fine with the tools, I'd just like fair warning.

headlineQuote: I'm fine with the tools, I'd just like fair warning.
portrait: Tara is a **24-year-old** cybersecurity master's student in Aarhus, with a software engineering degree and a testing internship.
She is a pragmatic centrist who uses AI **now and then** and picks careers by looking at job ads.
She owes about **fifteen thousand**, lives in student housing and relies on her boyfriend Anders for perspective.
Her steady style means she moves **when it's proven**, and she hedges with trades and savings.
She stays calm with time and turns **alarmed** only at two years.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, because it would hit before she'd had a real job.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear hiring information** from firms, flexible loan terms and a chance to try a trade.
